An Ethereum Foundation researcher suggests pre-transferring large sums to addresses that have not yet signed any transactions

On October 7th, Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake called on the crypto industry to calmly prepare for a scenario in which the ECDSA signature scheme could be hacked before the advent of a quantum computer. In his estimation, in the worst case, this could be a matter of months, not years. There is no confirmed method for such a hack.

Drake described the hack as rapid recovery of a private key from an already disclosed public one: for example, in about a week with available hardware such as a large cluster of graphics processors. According to him, it is now reasonable to prepare for such a possibility. He linked the warning to recent progress in mathematical models, including the publication of a set of mathematical works by OpenAI's internal model. The main risk, according to Drake, concerns addresses that have already signed transactions and thus revealed their public key. He recommends that large and prepared holders transfer most of their funds to addresses that have not signed anything yet. After each outgoing transaction, it is also better to transfer the remainder to a new address. You don't need a new wallet for this: you can get the address from the same seed phrase.

Drake specifically asks not to rush. According to him, there is cause for action, but a hasty transfer can do more harm than good. For wallets with less than 50 bitcoins, he sees partial coverage in already disclosed Satoshi addresses: around 20 thousand addresses with 50 bitcoins each. For oracle operators and second-layer network security advisors, he recommends changing the ECDSA key after each signed message or supplementing the signature with a hash-based scheme, such as SPHINCS.

According to his estimation, one can only exit this regime with cryptography designed for the period after the current development of artificial intelligence. Drake himself leans towards hash-based schemes and moving away from cryptography that relies on elliptic curves, lattices, or isogenies. In November, he plans to discuss the topic with institutional participants at a meeting in London.

📌 Market Cap vs Liquidity: Why a “Big Project” Can Still Be Thin

Main Points
⏺ Market cap is price × circulating supply, but it doesn’t show real tradable depth
⏺ Liquidity tells you how much can be bought/sold without moving price too much
⏺ This post explains why beginners must separate “valuation” from “liquidity”

1️⃣ Market Cap — a snapshot based on last traded price, not cash sitting in the book.
2️⃣ Liquidity — real depth: how much volume the market absorbs without heavy slippage.
3️⃣ Thin Markets — small flows can push price up and create a shiny market cap.
4️⃣ Exit Risk — entering is easy, exiting is hard; selling moves price faster than you expect.
5️⃣ Practical Check — watch volume, order book/pool depth, and spreads, not just market cap.

Final Thoughts

Market cap is the sign on the building. Liquidity is the door. If the door is narrow, exiting cleanly can be impossible.

Spain exempts self-custody wallets from crypto tax reporting

Spain's tax authorities have confirmed that cryptocurrency held in self-custody wallets — where the owner controls the private keys — does not need to be reported under Form 721, the country's disclosure form for foreign-held digital assets. The exemption hinges on one condition: no third party holds the assets on your behalf.

The rule draws a clean line between personal custody and exchange or custodial holdings abroad, which remain reportable. Simple in principle, potentially significant in practice — Spain just gave self-custody a regulatory edge.

Bill Pulte and the question of who is positioning for powerBill Pulte has emerged as one of the names associated with speculation about a possible change in the White House leadership structure. That speculation has drawn attention to the relationships and conversations surrounding the president’s advisers. 

Corey Lewandowski, a longtime Trump ally and former campaign manager, rejected one specific claim about Pulte’s prospects. “I have never spoken with the president about Bill Pulte being the chief of staff.”

The statement is a direct denial of a conversation that would have been relevant to succession speculation. It does not, by itself, resolve the broader question of who might be considered for a senior position if Wiles’ status changes. 

That distinction matters in an administration where rumors about personnel can become politically consequential before any formal decision is made. A name circulating among insiders may reflect genuine interest, informal speculation or an attempt by competing factions to shape perceptions of who is gaining ground.

Without confirmation from the president, the individuals involved or an official announcement, the succession question remains open.

The White House has pushed back against portrayals of the administration as divided by a struggle for control. Responding to the reporting, White House spokesman Davis Ingle dismissed the credibility of anonymous sources, saying: “These anonymous sources know nothing.”

The response reflects the administration’s effort to challenge accounts of internal conflict and reject the suggestion that outside observers have a reliable picture of its private deliberations. That denial is an important part of the story. 

Reports of internal rivalries often rely on people familiar with private conversations, and their accounts may reflect incomplete information, personal grievances or competing political interests. 

At the same time, official denials do not automatically settle questions about internal disagreements. The available evidence supports a more limited conclusion: succession speculation exists, the administration has faced questions about competing centers of influence, and the White House disputes the characterization of its internal dynamics as a power struggle. Whether those tensions will produce personnel changes remains uncertain. 

A network of allies, advisers and competing interestsThe struggle surrounding Wiles also illustrates the complexity of Trump’s wider political network. Formal government positions are only one source of influence. 

Longtime allies, former campaign officials and outside advisers can retain access to the president, creating additional channels through which competing arguments reach the White House. Lewandowski’s involvement in the wider political conversation is one example of how relationships outside the formal chain of command can become relevant to questions about senior staffing.

The reporting has also drawn attention to overseas consulting activities involving political strategists James Blair and Chris LaCivita, both associated with Wiles. Those activities have attracted scrutiny, adding another complication to the political environment surrounding figures close to the chief of staff. 

A change in the chief of staff’s office could alter the flow of information to Trump, redistribute influence among senior advisers and reshape how the White House responds to congressional opposition. The midterms will determine the balance of power on Capitol Hill. They may also become the moment when the president decides which people he trusts to manage the next phase of his administration.

Inside the West Wing, that possibility is enough to make every personnel rumor, public denial and sign of shifting allegiance politically significant.
